mesoscaleDiscussions.areas: Far northeast Colorado...southwest Nebraska...and far northwest Kansas
mesoscaleDiscussions.summary: Some threat for severe wind will continue across portions of far northeast Colorado and southwest Nebraska for the next couple of hours. There is some potential for a continuation of severe winds into portions of far northwest Kansas later tonight, but confidence in this threat is limited.

details.label: Areas affected
details.text: Far northeast Colorado...southwest Nebraska...and far northwest Kansas

details.label: Discussion
details.text: Over the past two hours, convection within a loosely organized band of storms has largely evolved as expected with the strongest cores now residing in far northeast CO - largely owing to the effects of increasing inhibition with eastward extent towards the North Platte, NE area. Despite this contraction in the band, latest echo top and GOES IR trends continue to show robust updraft development within the remaining cluster, suggesting that the near-storm environment across northeast CO/southwest NE remains supportive for intense convection. Additionally, KGLD velocity imagery shows hints of an emerging outflow surge, suggesting that this cluster will continue to pose a threat for severe wind, and perhaps transient hail, for the next hour or two as it continues to migrate across a relatively buoyant environment. Recent runs of the HRRR and RRFS both suggest that this cluster will continue to intensify with an expanding wind field through roughly 05-07 UTC as it spreads into southwest NE and far northwest KS. However, both of these solutions have been depicting broad cold pools with temperatures in the 65-70 F range. Surface observations have mostly been reporting cold pool temperatures in the 70-75 F range, suggesting that the modeled cold pools may be too deep/intense compared to reality. Consequently, this casts uncertainty on how widespread and intense the wind threat will be beyond the next 1-2 hours. Nonetheless, the downstream environment into northwest KS features only weak/shallow capping and MLCAPE values of around 2500 J/kg, which may support at least an isolated severe wind threat beyond WW 549. Convective trends will continue to be monitored, and downstream watch issuance is possible.

mesoscaleDiscussions.areas: Southeast Nebraska into northeast Kansas...northwest Missouri...and southwest Iowa
mesoscaleDiscussions.summary: A localized corridor of severe hail and wind potential may emerge over the next few hours across southeast Nebraska, northeast Kansas, and into adjacent portions of northwest Missouri and southwest Iowa. However, this threat will likely remain sufficiently isolated to preclude watch issuance.

details.label: Areas affected
details.text: Southeast Nebraska into northeast Kansas...northwest Missouri...and southwest Iowa

details.label: Discussion
details.text: Convective trends have been monitored over the past hour as an isolated thunderstorm developed across far southeast NE and crossed the MO River. More recently, additional attempts at deep convection are noted in radar and GOES IR imagery, and appear to be driven by strengthening isentropic ascent across a warm frontal zone as the nocturnal jet begins to slowly intensify (0-2 km winds have been increasing to 30-40 knots in upstream VWPs over the past 30-45 minutes). Despite a somewhat focused zone for initiation, the placement of this zone within the upper-level ridge axis suggests synoptic-scale forcing for ascent and deep-layer wind shear is limited for storm maintenance and/or intensification. The relatively short lifespan and recent demise of the initial cell crossing the MO River reflects these mitigating factors, despite an otherwise highly favorable thermodynamic environment (MUCAPE analyzed upwards of 4000-5000 J/kg). Over the next few hours, the expectation is for additional development of isolated cells and perhaps a few clusters to the north of the surface warm front. Very strong instability will favor robust updraft development that may pose a threat for isolated large hail and perhaps strong to severe downbursts. However, given the buoyancy-driven nature of this convection within a modestly sheared environment, storm organization and longevity may be limited. Furthermore, this activity should primarily reside within an MUCIN minimum co-located with the strongest isentropic ascent. Storm maintenance out of this corridor seems unlikely, and should spatially confine the severe threat. Given these limitations, watch issuance is not anticipated.
